title: Der Wolf und der Mensch
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 72. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original scans). 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng, Thier, todt).
about: KHM 72, a short beast-fable in which the wolf refuses to take the fox’s warning about man on trust and goes to see for himself. Its pleasure is the wolf’s report at the end: having no word for a gun or a blade, he can only describe a stick that is blown into and a bright rib drawn out of a body. Spelling follows the 1857 edition, so you will meet older forms such as Thier, gieng, Schade and todt.

sentences.t: Der Fuchs erzählte einmal dem Wolf von der Stärke des Menschen, kein Thier könnte ihm widerstehen, und sie müßten List gebrauchen, um sich vor ihm zu erhalten.
sentences.l: The fox once told the wolf of the strength of man: no animal could withstand him, and they would have to use cunning in order to preserve themselves from him.
sentences.i: The fox was once telling the wolf about the strength of man — no beast could stand against him, and they would have to use cunning to keep themselves safe from him.
sentences.n: Mensch is the human being as such, not the male; the whole joke of the tale is that the wolf has never met one. könnte and müßten are subjunctive: from the comma onward the sentence is still the fox speaking, reported rather than quoted.

sentences.t: Da antwortete der Wolf „wenn ich nur einmal einen Menschen zu sehen bekäme, ich wollte doch auf ihn losgehen.“
sentences.l: Then the wolf answered “if I only once got a man to see, I would go at him all the same.”
sentences.i: Then the wolf answered: “If I could just once get sight of a man, I would go at him for all that.”
sentences.n: “zu sehen bekommen” — to get to see, to catch sight of. losgehen auf jemanden, to go straight at someone, runs through the tale and is separable.

sentences.t: „Dazu kann ich dir helfen,“ sprach der Fuchs, „komm nur morgen früh zu mir, so will ich dir einen zeigen.“
sentences.l: “With that I can help you,” said the fox, “only come to me tomorrow early, then I will show you one.”
sentences.i: “I can help you to that,” said the fox. “Just come to me early tomorrow, and I will show you one.”
sentences.n: The resumptive so after an imperative — “komm nur …, so will ich” — is old-fashioned; modern German drops it. will here is intention, not the future.

sentences.t: Der Wolf stellte sich frühzeitig ein, und der Fuchs brachte ihn hinaus auf den Weg, den der Jäger alle Tage gieng.
sentences.l: The wolf presented himself early, and the fox brought him out onto the path that the huntsman went every day.
sentences.i: The wolf turned up in good time, and the fox brought him out to the path the huntsman walked every day.
sentences.n: “sich einstellen” — to present oneself, to turn up at an appointed place; the reflexive is what makes it mean this. “alle Tage” for modern jeden Tag.

sentences.t: Zuerst kam ein alter abgedankter Soldat.
sentences.l: First came an old discharged soldier.
sentences.n: abgedankt — paid off, discharged from service. The pensioned-off soldier tramping the roads was a familiar sight in the Grimms’ Germany, and he turns up in a good many of the tales.

sentences.t: „Ist das ein Mensch?“ fragte der Wolf.
sentences.l: “Is that a man?” asked the wolf.

sentences.t: „Nein,“ antwortete der Fuchs, „das ist einer gewesen.“
sentences.l: “No,” answered the fox, “that has been one.”
sentences.i: “No,” answered the fox, “that was one once.”
sentences.n: einer is the pronoun “a one,” taking the ending the article would have had. The perfect “ist … gewesen” stands where English wants a plain past — he was one, in his time.

sentences.t: Danach kam ein kleiner Knabe, der zur Schule wollte.
sentences.l: After that came a small boy who wanted to school.
sentences.i: After that came a small boy on his way to school.
sentences.n: zur Schule wollte drops the verb of motion after the modal: wanted [to go] to school. German leaves gehen out freely in this construction.

sentences.l: “No, that wants first to become one.”
sentences.i: “No, that one has yet to become one.”

sentences.t: Endlich kam der Jäger, die Doppelflinte auf dem Rücken, und den Hirschfänger an der Seite.
sentences.l: At last came the huntsman, the double-barrelled gun on his back, and the hunting-knife at his side.
sentences.n: Hirschfänger — literally a “stag-catcher,” the short heavy blade a huntsman carried to finish wounded game. The wolf will describe it at the end without knowing what it is.

sentences.t: Sprach der Fuchs zum Wolf „siehst du, dort kommt ein Mensch, auf den mußt du losgehen, ich aber will mich fort in meine Höhle machen.“
sentences.l: Said the fox to the wolf “do you see, there comes a man, at him you must go; but I will make myself off into my den.”
sentences.i: Said the fox to the wolf: “You see, there comes a man — at him you must go; but I shall take myself off into my den.”
sentences.n: “sich fort machen” — to make off, to clear out; the reflexive mich and the particle fort both wait in the middle while the infinitive machen goes last.

sentences.t: Der Wolf gieng nun auf den Menschen los, der Jäger, als er ihn erblickte, sprach „es ist Schade, daß ich keine Kugel geladen habe,“ legte an und schoß dem Wolf das Schrot ins Gesicht.
sentences.l: The wolf now went at the man; the huntsman, when he caught sight of him, said “it is a pity that I have loaded no ball,” levelled his gun and shot the shot into the wolf’s face.
sentences.i: The wolf now went at the man; and the huntsman, catching sight of him, said, “It is a shame I have no ball loaded,” took aim, and fired the small shot into the wolf’s face.
sentences.n: Kugel is a single ball, Schrot the scattering pellets meant for birds — the huntsman is complaining that he has only the lighter load in the barrel. anlegen (to level a gun) is separable: “legte an.”

sentences.t: Der Wolf verzog das Gesicht gewaltig, doch ließ er sich nicht schrecken und gieng vorwärts: da gab ihm der Jäger die zweite Ladung.
sentences.l: The wolf pulled his face mightily out of shape, yet he did not let himself be frightened and went forward: then the huntsman gave him the second charge.
sentences.i: The wolf’s face twisted horribly, but he would not be frightened off and came on; whereupon the huntsman gave him the second barrel.
sentences.n: “das Gesicht verziehen” — to pull one’s face out of shape, to grimace. “sich nicht schrecken lassen” uses lassen where English uses a passive: he would not let himself be frightened.

sentences.t: Der Wolf verbiß den Schmerz und rückte dem Jäger zu Leibe: da zog dieser seinen blanken Hirschfänger und gab ihm links und rechts ein paar Hiebe, daß er, über und über blutend, mit Geheul zu dem Fuchs zurück lief.
sentences.l: The wolf bit back the pain and moved up to the huntsman’s body: then this one drew his bright hunting-knife and gave him a couple of strokes left and right, so that he, bleeding over and over, ran back to the fox with howling.
sentences.i: The wolf bit back the pain and closed with the huntsman; whereupon the huntsman drew his bright hunting-knife and dealt him a few strokes left and right, so that he ran back to the fox howling and covered in blood.
sentences.n: “einem zu Leibe rücken” — to move up to someone’s body, i.e. to close with him. dieser (“this one”) picks out the nearer of the two just named, the huntsman.

sentences.t: „Nun, Bruder Wolf,“ sprach der Fuchs, „wie bist du mit dem Menschen fertig worden?“
sentences.l: “Well, brother wolf,” said the fox, “how did you get finished with the man?”
sentences.i: “Well now, brother wolf,” said the fox, “how did you come off with your man?”
sentences.n: fertig werden mit — to get to the end of something, to be done with it, and of an opponent to get the better of him. worden is the older participle of werden where modern German writes geworden; the short form now survives only where werden is the passive auxiliary.

sentences.t: „Ach,“ antwortete der Wolf, „so hab ich mir die Stärke des Menschen nicht vorgestellt, erst nahm er einen Stock von der Schulter und blies hinein, da flog mir etwas ins Gesicht, das hat mich ganz entsetzlich gekitzelt:
sentences.l: “Alas,” answered the wolf, “so I have not pictured to myself the strength of man; first he took a stick from his shoulder and blew into it, then something flew into my face that tickled me quite dreadfully:
sentences.i: “Alas,” answered the wolf, “this is not how I had imagined the strength of man. First he took a stick from his shoulder and blew into it, and something flew into my face and tickled me most dreadfully;
sentences.n: The wolf has no words for a gun, so he reports only what he saw. gekitzelt, “tickled,” is his own understatement — he is bleeding from it.

sentences.t: danach pustete er noch einmal in den Stock, da flog mirs um die Nase, wie Blitz und Hagelwetter, und wie ich ganz nah war, da zog er eine blanke Rippe aus dem Leib, damit hat er so auf mich losgeschlagen, daß ich beinah todt wäre liegen geblieben.“
sentences.l: afterwards he puffed once more into the stick, then it flew about my nose like lightning and hailstorm, and when I was quite near, then he drew a bright rib out of his body; with that he struck at me so that I would nearly have been left lying dead.”
sentences.i: then he puffed into the stick once more, and it came about my nose like lightning and hail; and when I was quite close he drew a bright rib out of his body, and laid about me with it so that I was very nearly left lying there dead.”
sentences.n: The “bright rib out of his body” is the Hirschfänger, drawn from the sheath at the huntsman’s side; the wolf can only take a blade out of a man for a bone out of a man. todt is the 1857 spelling of tot.

sentences.t: „Siehst du,“ sprach der Fuchs, „was du für ein Prahlhans bist: du wirfst das Beil so weit, daß dus nicht wieder holen kannst.“
sentences.l: “Do you see,” said the fox, “what a braggart you are: you throw the axe so far that you cannot fetch it back again.”
sentences.i: “You see,” said the fox, “what a boaster you are: you throw the axe so far that you cannot go and get it again.”
sentences.n: Prahlhans — a “boasting Hans”: German builds a type by hanging the trait on its commonest given name, as it does in Hanswurst and Schmalhans. The closing line has the shape of a proverb — throwing further than you can walk to fetch. dus is du es run together.
